title: Caching
summary: Put a cache on a hot read and choose invalidation before quoting hit rate.

parts.rule: Add a cache only on a measured or estimated hot read path. Decide what is stored (object, row, rendered page), the exact key, the TTL, and how writes invalidate or refresh that key. Say what a client can observe on a stale hit. Hit-rate talk comes after the invalidation story, never before it.
parts.why: Caches without invalidation invent subtle bugs: deleted short links that still redirect, or catalog prices that lag for minutes. Interviewers probe consistency more than they admire a Redis logo. Naming TTL versus explicit delete shows you see the failure mode.
parts.example: Shortener redirect cache: key equals code, value equals long_url, TTL twenty-four hours. On create you may warm the cache. On delete or URL change, delete the cache key before acknowledging the write, or consciously accept stale redirects until TTL expiry. Walk the crash race: database updated, process dies before cache delete — readers may see the old URL until TTL; state that tradeoff. For user profiles at about twenty thousand reads per second with only a thousand distinct active users, an LRU memory cache in front of SQL collapses origin load. Do not cache the entire database as one blob; cache by the access key you already named in the data model lesson.
parts.use: Cache after the read path exists and QPS justifies the extra moving part. Prefer explicit invalidation on correctness-critical writes; prefer TTL on data that may be briefly stale. Place the cache beside the service that owns the read.
parts.refuse: Refuse drawing a cache as the first component on the whiteboard. Refuse claiming strong consistency while using TTL-only invalidation. Refuse caching writes that must be durable with no database underneath. Refuse a single global cache key that becomes a hot lock.

body:
Rule. Add a cache only on a measured or estimated hot read path. Decide what is stored (object, row, rendered page), the exact key, the TTL, and how writes invalidate or refresh that key. Say what a client can observe on a stale hit. Hit-rate talk comes after the invalidation story, never before it.

Why it matters. Caches without invalidation invent subtle bugs: deleted short links that still redirect, or catalog prices that lag for minutes. Interviewers probe consistency more than they admire a Redis logo. Naming TTL versus explicit delete shows you see the failure mode.

Worked example. Shortener redirect cache: key equals code, value equals long_url, TTL twenty-four hours. On create you may warm the cache. On delete or URL change, delete the cache key before acknowledging the write, or consciously accept stale redirects until TTL expiry. Walk the crash race: database updated, process dies before cache delete — readers may see the old URL until TTL; state that tradeoff. For user profiles at about twenty thousand reads per second with only a thousand distinct active users, an LRU memory cache in front of SQL collapses origin load. Do not cache the entire database as one blob; cache by the access key you already named in the data model lesson.

When to use. Cache after the read path exists and QPS justifies the extra moving part. Prefer explicit invalidation on correctness-critical writes; prefer TTL on data that may be briefly stale. Place the cache beside the service that owns the read.

When to refuse. Refuse drawing a cache as the first component on the whiteboard. Refuse claiming strong consistency while using TTL-only invalidation. Refuse caching writes that must be durable with no database underneath. Refuse a single global cache key that becomes a hot lock.
